description: Believes a variable stores the expression it was assigned rather than its value, so it changes when the variables in that expression change later.
Believes b = a links the two variables, so a later change to a also changes b.
Believes a = b copies the value of a into b, as if assignment worked from left to right.
Believes a variable keeps the first value it was given and later assignments to it have no effect.
Believes = compares two values instead of storing the right-hand value in the variable.
Believes an expression such as x + 1 written on its own line updates the variable x.
Believes / between two integers gives a whole number by dropping the remainder.
Believes the % operator gives the result of the division rather than the remainder.
Believes two separate if statements in a row behave like if/elif, so once the first one runs the second is skipped.
Believes every branch of an if/elif chain whose condition is true runs, not just the first one.
Believes the else branch always runs after the if branch, whether or not the condition was true.
Believes that if an if condition is false and there is no else, the program stops and the lines after the if block do not run.
Believes the lines after an if block belong to it and only run when the condition is true, even though they are not indented.
Believes the body of an if statement keeps repeating for as long as its condition stays true.
Believes x == 1 or 2 checks whether x equals 1 or x equals 2.
Believes and and or always evaluate both sides, even when the left side already decides the result.
Believes 0, an empty string, or an empty list counts as True in a condition because the value exists.
Believes range(n) counts from 1 to n.
Believes range(n) counts from 0 up to and including n.
Believes in range(a, b) the second number is how many values to produce starting from a.
Believes each pass through a loop starts again from the values the variables had before the loop, so updates do not carry over.
Believes a for loop runs its body only once, using the last value in the sequence.
Believes each statement in a loop body is repeated all its times before the next statement starts.
Believes a statement placed right after a loop, without indentation, is also repeated on every pass of the loop.
Believes a while loop runs its body at most once, like an if statement.
Believes a while loop stops the moment its condition becomes false, even partway through the body.
Believes that after for i in range(n) finishes, i holds the value n.
Believes break exits every loop it is nested in, not just the innermost one.
Believes break only skips the rest of the current pass and the loop then carries on with the next value.
Believes print inside a function sends the value back to the caller, the same as return.
Believes return displays the value on the screen even when the result of the call is not printed.
Believes a function with no return statement gives back the last value it computed instead of None.
Believes a return in the middle of a function does not end it, and the remaining lines still run.
Believes a return inside a called function also ends the function that called it.
Believes the body of a function runs as soon as it is defined, even if it is never called.
Believes a function that takes no arguments can be called by writing its name without parentheses.
Believes assigning a new value to a parameter inside a function changes the variable that was passed in.
Believes assigning to a variable inside a function changes the variable with the same name outside it.
Believes arguments are matched to parameters by their variable names rather than by their position.
Believes in a nested call like f(g(x)) the outer function runs before the inner one.
Believes b = a makes a separate copy of a list, so changing b leaves a unchanged.
Believes a function receives its own copy of a list argument, so changing the list inside the function does not affect the caller's list.
Believes list and string positions start at 1, so lst[1] is the first element.
Believes the last element of a list is at index len(lst).
Believes a slice lst[a:b] includes the element at index b.
Believes lst.append(x) returns the updated list, so lst = lst.append(x) keeps the list.
Believes lst.sort() returns the sorted list, so its result can be assigned or printed.
Believes calling sorted(lst) rearranges lst itself, even when the result is not stored.
Believes + between two lists adds matching elements together instead of joining the lists.
Believes for x in lst gives the positions of the items rather than the items themselves.
Believes for i in range(len(lst)) gives the items of the list rather than their positions.
Believes string methods like upper() or replace() change the original string, even when the result is not stored.
Believes comparing two strings with < or > compares their lengths.
Believes strings made of digits are compared by their numeric value rather than character by character.
Believes + on two strings made of digits adds them as numbers instead of joining them.
Believes multiplying a string of digits by an integer multiplies the number instead of repeating the string.
Believes joining strings with + automatically puts a space between them.
Believes print(a, b) prints the values right next to each other with no space between them.
Believes in s[a:b] the second number is how many characters to take starting at position a.
Believes putting a variable's name in quotes still refers to its value, so print('x') shows what x holds.
Made a careless slip such as a typo or an arithmetic error while understanding the concept correctly.
Believes that the while loop body never executes and only the final print statement runs.
Assumes that using range(len(fruits)) iterates over the fruit values instead of their index numbers.
